detail: Algorithmic fairness, game theory, and machine learning for the allocation of scarce societal resources
Interpretable models of human discretion in public-sector decision-making
Evaluation and reliability of large language models for high-stakes judgments
Learning dynamics in two-sided matching markets
Advanced to candidacy in September 2026 after defending the dissertation proposal

Designed a two-arm study to test procedural equivalence in constructing rater-calibration “training packs” for a state reading assessment: an observational contrast of historical human-built versus current model-assisted packs, and a prospective controlled comparison across human-only, model-assisted, and consensus-gold processes; framed the question as a non-inferiority estimand and specified deconfounding strategies to unalias the manual-vs-model contrast from year.

Developed a response-agnostic Wasserstein distance over ordinal score-band labels to compare pack profiles without requiring shared responses, and built the surrounding inference framework (TOST equivalence testing with a margin scaled to observed human pack spread, estimated in a mixed model with item and rater random effects).

Applied post-hoc interpretability methods (integrated gradients, counterfactual perturbation, probing classifiers, collinearity-stable relative-importance analysis) to a proprietary transformer scorer with no exposed internals, characterizing the linguistic cues associated with score assignments.

Engineered a reproducible analysis pipeline (Python 3.12) with a synthetic-data generator, a single configuration flag to switch between simulated and production data, pinned dependency lockfiles, and drift-blocking pre-commit hooks; validated the full pipeline on simulated data ahead of data-collection approval.

Authored a technical methods note and a pre-registration of the primary estimand and equivalence margin, and produced operational briefing materials for experienced scorers and an independent gold panel; presented the study design to research and operations stakeholders.
Built and validated models of real-world human decision-making using large, noisy administrative datasets; emphasized replicable pipelines, clear error analysis, and decision-relevant metrics.

Developed interpretable ML baselines (short decision trees) to approximate “default” judgment policies and quantified systematic deviations; used this framework to study consistency and outcome correlates of overrides.
Designed evaluation protocols for AI judgment systems (including repeated-run robustness checks, aggregation from pairwise preferences to global rankings, and structured failure-mode analysis).
Implemented simulation and sequential decision-making methods (bandits / learning dynamics) relevant to adaptive sampling strategies and resource allocation under uncertainty.
Produced well-documented Python tooling for data preparation, feature generation, model training, and reporting to support iterative experimentation with strict temporal separation.
Supported instruction for graduate ML (office hours, grading, exam logistics); strengthened communication of technical ideas and careful evaluation practice.
